---
title = "Calepin vs Quarto"
---

*Calepin* aims for (nearly) full compatibility with [Quarto](https://quarto.org/)'s `.qmd` syntax, but makes different design choices. This page explains the main differences.


# Architecture

Quarto delegates most of its parsing and format conversion to [Pandoc](https://pandoc.org/). This gives Quarto access to Pandoc's many output formats (EPUB, DOCX, ODT, etc.), but it also means that Quarto's rendering speed is bounded by Pandoc's.

*Calepin* does not use Pandoc. Markdown parsing (via comrak), code execution, citation processing, cross-references, and template rendering are all implemented in Rust within a single binary. This makes *Calepin* much faster, but it currently supports fewer output formats: HTML, LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown.


# Performance

Quarto typically renders a document in seconds. *Calepin* renders the same document in milliseconds (excluding code execution time, which is the same in both).

This difference matters in practice. With *Calepin*, the live preview server can re-render and reload the browser instantly every time you save a file. For large websites with hundreds of pages, the difference between seconds-per-page and milliseconds-per-page is the difference between a minutes-long build and one that finishes before you can switch to your browser.

Note that [Quarto 2](https://quarto.org/) is in development and should offer performance in the same class as *Calepin*.


# Configuration: YAML vs TOML

Quarto uses YAML front matter. *Calepin* uses TOML front matter:

```toml
---
title = "My Document"
author = "Jane Doe"
bibliography = "refs.bib"
number-sections = true
---
```

Structured metadata like authors with affiliations works naturally:

```toml
[[author]]
name = "Jane Doe"

[[author.affiliations]]
name = "University of Montreal"
department = "Department of Computer Science"
```

This is an intentional break from Quarto. Not all of the hundreds of configuration options available in Quarto's YAML should be expected to work in *Calepin*. Using a different format makes that clear upfront.

Beyond signaling, I just personally prefer working with TOML. It avoids the type, structure, and white-space related headaches that YAML is notorious for, and it has become the standard configuration format in the Python and Rust ecosystems (for good reasons).

In future versions of *Calepin*, we may (or may not) add a compatibility layer with support for YAML front matter.

# Customization philosophy

Both Quarto and *Calepin* use templates to control output. In Quarto, templates are written in Pandoc's template language; in *Calepin*, they are Jinja2 templates, which are more expressive (conditionals, loops, filters, macros, template inheritance). Both systems let you override individual templates to customize the look of your documents.

The difference is one of emphasis. Quarto offers hundreds of YAML front matter keys that control layout, styling, and behavior, and most users rely on those keys rather than editing templates directly. *Calepin* offers fewer configuration keys and instead encourages you to edit the templates themselves. The templates are simple HTML, LaTeX, or Typst files with `{{ variable }}` placeholders.

This design is especially well-suited to working with LLMs. Since templates are just plain text in well-known formats, you can describe what you want and let your LLM agent customize your website, templates, and styles directly:

> Go to the `index_calepin/templates` folder. Switch all the colors to a pastel theme. Make the top navigation bar twice as wide. Align the footer text to the right.


# Documentation extraction

*Calepin* includes built-in documentation extraction for R and Python packages via the `calepin man` command. It parses R help files (Rd) and Python docstrings (Google, NumPy, Sphinx, and Markdown styles) and generates `.qmd` reference pages automatically. This means *Calepin* can act as a replacement for dedicated documentation tools like [pkgdown](https://pkgdown.r-lib.org/) (R) or [MkDocs](https://www.mkdocs.org/) (Python), while also supporting executable code chunks, cross-references, and citations in the same project.


# Bootstrap vs. Tailwind CSS

Quarto's HTML output is built on [Bootstrap 5](https://getbootstrap.com/), with an SCSS theming system for overriding variables. *Calepin* uses [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) utility classes instead. All styling lives directly in the HTML templates, so customization means editing templates rather than writing SCSS. The framework is very easy to learn and extremely flexible, as demonstrated in the [Tailwind CSS](../websites/tailwind.qmd) section. This works especially well with LLM assistants, since the agent can read a single HTML file and understand exactly how it is styled.


# Extensions directory

Quarto uses `_extensions/` for custom formats and filters. *Calepin* uses `{stem}_calepin/templates/` for template overrides and `{stem}_calepin/extensions/` for custom [extensions](../extensions/extensions.qmd). The two extension systems are incompatible.
